source.title: When Words Are Safe But Actions Kill: Probing Physical Jailbreak Beyond Textual Jailbreak in Hidden-State Risk Space
source.authors: Weimeng Wang; Zi-Qiang Wang; Zi-Hang Zhan; Chuan-Pu Fu; Qi Li; Ke Xu

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the single-refusal-direction finding in related work but does not test or rely on that refusal mechanism. Its own experiments examine textual-jailbreak and physical-jailbreak representations and instruction classification, not refusal behavior.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no refusal-direction ablation or addition, no refusal-rate outcome, and no test of the refusal direction as a weight edit or jailbreak mechanism. The rows below record the adjacent textual-versus-physical-jailbreak representation results; they do not test a claim version. Layer-selection sweep values and cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Arditi et al. once in related work, as an example of a single refusal direction. Its own experiments probe hidden-state directions separating textual- from physical-jailbreak instructions, against safe instructions. It reports no refusal rate. It does no ablation or addition of a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, and no weight edit. Its 'jailbreak' means unsafe embodied instructions, not attacks that suppress refusal. The TJD/PJD directions are labelled-class mean or probe directions used for detection, not directions shown to mediate refusal behaviour.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that textual- and physical-jailbreak signals are separable in hidden states (beyond a random-split null on Qwen2.5-3B, with consistent angle patterns elsewhere). They find a single-layer logistic probe (PRISM) detects both with lower false-positive rates than LLM judges. On the lexically controlled PJB pool the signal is real but imperfect (0.718 cell-grouped AUC). They draw no conclusion about refusal mediation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures class-mean and logistic-probe directions for textual versus physical jailbreak and trains a full-state safety classifier. It does not find or intervene on a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported probe layer is selected per model; the paper reports different selected layers across model sizes and architectures. Its cross-dataset results use within-dataset training rather than zero-shot transfer.

fits_no_version.finding: Textual-jailbreak and physical-jailbreak unsafe-vs-safe directions are separated: probe-weight angles are about 71–77° across six models, and mean-difference angles 33–68°. For Qwen2.5-3B the angle exceeds a random-split null (z=10.09).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different kinds of unsafe instruction (explicitly worded vs. physically grounded hazards) occupy distinct linear directions in hidden states, rather than one generic unsafe axis.

fits_no_version.finding: A probe trained on safe vs. textual jailbreak detects only 19.8–32.6% of physical jailbreaks out of distribution. A probe trained on safe vs. physical jailbreak detects 68.1–85.0% of textual jailbreaks in the reverse direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear detectors for one class of unsafe instruction transfer incompletely to another class.

record.problems: The paper explicitly notes that the random-split null test was completed only for Qwen2.5-3B, so cross-model angle patterns are descriptive. Several evaluation results use selected-layer estimates rather than fully nested layer selection. The experiments concern jailbreak-label detection and representation geometry, not refusal behavior or general capability.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; fewer than 60 rows were recorded. Other classifier performance and benchmark results were omitted because they do not directly bear on the adjacent direction-separation finding or on the refusal claim.

untested.parts: Refusal direction extraction, ablation or addition effects on refusal, capability retention
Weight-edit abliteration and refusal in released models
Whether attacks suppress the refusal direction; adversarial training against ablation
Separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision
Refusal direction transfer across languages, variants, or base to instruct
Role of training in forming a removable refusal direction

missing.what: Out-of-distribution TJD→PJ and PJD→TJ detection rates for Phi-3.5-mini (38.0/67.3%) and SmolLM2-1.7B (25.7/71.7%). These are adjacent findings only and bear on no version.

record.verdict_notes: The study's 'jailbreak' denotes unsafe instructions, not attacks on refusal. Its single-direction language concerns detection probes, not refusal behaviour, so none of V1–V8 is tested. The random-split null exists only for 3B. Layer selection is not nested.

versions.untested_parts: Refusal-direction measurement, causal removal or addition, refusal behavior, and general capability.
Weight-edit ablation and refusal behavior in released models.
Whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or training against its ablation improves robustness.
Whether refusal is encoded by an affine set, cone, or dominant direction plus other refusal directions.
Whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are separately encoded.
Transfer of a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
Whether refusal training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.
